thread_title: S. leuco alba  'yellow flower,solid white' Washington Co, AL
breadcrumb: S. leuco alba  'yellow flower,solid white' Washington Co, AL

posts.body_html:
Now, it's hard to complain about having a yellow flowered variant that also is one of the whitest clones out there! This is one of the few individuals that rivals hurricane creek white clone F, and to make things even more interesting, these produce an abundance of very solid white summer traps! however, the fall traps are much bigger and even whiter!

My hope in the future is to breed for super solid white traps that have the pigments stretch far down the petiole. Fortunately, the washington Co, Al population has sufficient genetic ingredients to potentially make that plant, but as with all crosses, you never know what will happen until you jump in and try! I have yet to see, both in nature and in cultivation, a yellow flowered plant that has white stretch 2" or more down the petiole....wouldn't that be something?

Here's S. leucophylla var. alba 'yellow flower, solid white' Washington Co, AL. Edit: placed this photo just cuz the other earlier pics just don't show how ridiculously white this plant can get. Pic taken 9/2/17:








photos taken 8/2/17. Schnell's ghost looks sun-tanned compared to this thing, LOL

posts.body_html:
Calen-this year, it's been warmer up in Portland than where I am in northern Cali. Your average day and night temps are higher than here too! We've actually had a relatively cool summer so far, at least in my microclimate. The bananas grew must faster and bigger last year compared to this year. I'm curious as to what your humidity is like up there? Since you get more rain and moisture, maybe there's higher humidity, so the leucos aren't frying? They certainly don't fry in 102F heat waves in the wild....

Foe show, the washington Co plants color up way easier than many other populations. Looking forward to seeing how they do for you this fall, I think you'll have a great leuco year if the weather continues like this!

Word! We've been having an awesome summer. Very dry actually - we have had zero rain since the second week in June (while the summers here are dry, it's unusual to have NO rain...). Humidity is fairly low, comparable to warm dry weather in NorCal actually, but we certainly did get a later start and humidity was higher in May and June when there was still some moisture about the place.

I am definitely hoping for a warm, sunny September and great leucos. The only thing that could wrench that up is the fact that everything was so late to get going this year, especially the leucos. Time will tell if their internal clocks will give them enough time to pitcher. Many clones are just initiating phyllodia production now when they "should" have most of those fully grown by late July!

posts.body_html:
Hells yeah! Man, I am running quite a temperature with this leuco fever I've got right about now!

Mine is throwing up a nice flush currently with the first of what look like fall pitchers set to open any day. It's got the same bronze color to the green area under the white that Hurricane Creek Whites do, which is interesting. Seems like these alba types usually open with a few veins and then "infuse" solid white over a week or two if the light is bright.

posts.body_html:
Even bigger traps are on the way but here are a few nice transitional late summer traps on this awesome clone. It's so interesting how these Washington Co. plants continually grow traps and seem to "ramp up" to their fall traps rather than suddenly explode with a big flush. The trap on the left is the biggest and youngest and has yet to white-out completely. The middle trap is maybe 2 weeks old, and the small one lower right is a month old. 
IMG_1694 by Calen Hall, on Flickr
